entry: Indian nationalist and self-rule activist, known to his supporters as Lokmanya ("accepted by the people as their leader"). Tilak was one of the first and strongest advocates of *swaraj* ("self-rule") and is known for the declaration "Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it!" He was one of the Lal Bal Pal triumvirate with Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai. He joined the [[Indian National Congress]] in 1890, and the Swadeshi movement of 1905–1907 led to a split within it between moderates and extremists. His activism in the [[Indian independence movement]] led to several imprisonments, including a long stint at [[Mandalay]]. His *Gita Rahasya* (1915) interpreted the [[Bhagavad Gita]] as endorsing active duty without attachment. Historians have debated his politics: he has been considered a conservative reactionary, and scholar Biswamoy Pati argued that he "represented and articulated the interests of the bourgeoisie as a class in a colonial context."

[[Bird of prey]] species of North America, a sea eagle. Its range includes most of [[Canada]] and [[Alaska]], all of the contiguous [[United States]], and northern [[Mexico]]. It feeds mainly on fish and builds the largest nest of any North American bird. Adults have a brown body and a white head and tail. The bald eagle is the national bird and symbol of the United States. In the late 20th century it was on the brink of extirpation in the contiguous United States until bans on hunting and on the pesticide [[DDT]] slowed the decline. Its status was upgraded from endangered to threatened in 1995, and it was removed from the list in 2007.

Series of role-playing video games set in the Forgotten Realms campaign setting of [[Dungeons & Dragons]]. The Bhaalspawn Saga was developed by BioWare for [[Personal computer|personal computers]] and used pausable real-time gameplay, which is credited with revitalizing the computer role-playing game genre. *Baldur's Gate* was the third computer game to use the [[Lua]] scripting language. The Dark Alliance series was released for consoles. Larian Studios developed *Baldur's Gate 3*, released in 2023.

Archipelago in the western [[Mediterranean Sea]], forming an autonomous community and province of [[Spain]]. Its capital and largest city is Palma, on [[Mallorca]]. With a population of 1,249,844, the Balearic Islands are the 6th least populous autonomous community of Spain, and at 4,991.70 sq km they are the smallest. Historically part of the Kingdom of Majorca, they achieved self-government under a Statute of Autonomy in 1983. Catalan and Spanish are co-official languages. The western Pityusic Islands include [[Ibiza]] and Formentera, while the eastern Gymnesian Islands are principally Mallorca and Menorca. The region has a [[Mediterranean climate]], and Ibiza is known for electronic music and nightlife.

Public statement issued by the British government on November 2, 1917, supporting a "national home for the Jewish people" in [[Palestine (region)|Palestine]]. It took the form of a letter from Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour to Lord Rothschild, for transmission to the [[Zionism|Zionist]] Federation. Its opening words were the first public expression of support for Zionism by a major political power. The second half protected the civil and religious rights of the Palestinian Arabs, who formed the vast majority of the local population. The declaration became a core component of the British Mandate for [[Mandatory Palestine]] and indirectly led to the State of Israel. It is considered a principal cause of the [[Israeli–Palestinian conflict]], and controversy remains over whether it contradicted British promises to the Sharif of Mecca.

Indonesian island and province, the westernmost of the [[Lesser Sunda Islands]]. It is the only Hindu-majority province in Indonesia, with 86.40% of the population adhering to [[Hinduism|Balinese Hinduism]]. The province is Indonesia's main tourist destination, and tourism-related business makes up 80% of its economy. Bali is renowned for its arts, including dance, sculpture, painting and music. The Subak irrigation system is a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site. The name appears in ancient inscriptions as Vāli-dvīpa, and the Belanjong pillar inscription, dated to about 914 CE, is one of the earliest attestations. The population exceeded 4.4 million in 2024.

Theater of [[World War I]] between the [[Central Powers]] and the Allies. The campaign opened in 1914 with three failed Austro-Hungarian offensives into Serbia, which cost the Austro-Hungarians 100,000 troops on the first day. A combined Austro-Hungarian, German and Bulgarian offensive in 1915 conquered Serbia and Montenegro. The Serbian army retreated through Albania, was evacuated to [[Corfu]], and reformed at [[Thessaloniki|Salonika]]. Greece joined the Allies in 1917. In September 1918 the Vardar Offensive broke the Bulgarian lines, forcing Bulgaria to surrender, and Serbia, Albania and Montenegro were liberated soon after.

Mountain range of southeastern Europe, about 560 km long, from the Serbia–Bulgaria border to the Black Sea. The range forms a natural barrier between the northern and southern halves of Bulgaria, and its highest point is Botev Peak, at 2,376 m. In much of its central and eastern sections the summit forms the watershed between the Black Sea and Aegean drainage basins. The [[Karst|karst]] terrain contains many caves, including Magura, which has the most important extended European post-Palaeolithic cave painting. Central Balkan National Park has steep cliffs and the highest waterfalls in the Balkan region. Most of Europe's large mammals live in the range, including the [[Brown bear|brown bear]], wolf and deer. The mountains gave their name to the [[Balkans]].

Two conflicts in the Balkan states, 1912–1913. In the First Balkan War, Greece, Serbia, Montenegro and Bulgaria declared war on the [[Ottoman Empire]] and defeated it, leaving only Eastern Thrace under Ottoman control. The Treaty of London of May 30, 1913, included independence for [[Albania]]. The Second Balkan War began on June 16, 1913, when Bulgaria attacked its former allies. Romania invaded Bulgaria from the north, and the Ottoman Empire also attacked. The Treaty of Bucharest left Bulgaria with most of its gains from the first war but ceded southern Dobruja to Romania. The wars were marked by ethnic cleansing and atrocities by all parties, and they set the stage for the July crisis of 1914 and the [[World War I|First World War]].

Geographical region of southeastern Europe, partly corresponding to the Balkan Peninsula. The name derives from the [[Balkan Mountains]], which stretch across Bulgaria. The peninsula is bounded by the [[Adriatic Sea]], Ionian Sea, Aegean Sea, Turkish Straits and Black Sea. The German geographer August Zeune created the concept in 1808, and in the 19th century the term was a synonym for Rumelia, the provinces of the [[Ottoman Empire]] in Europe. Modern geographers reject the Balkan Peninsula as a geographic unit, and the term has acquired a pejorative meaning linked to Balkanization. By most definitions the region includes Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Greece, Kosovo, Montenegro and North Macedonia, along with parts of Croatia, Romania, Serbia and Turkey.

Round object, usually spherical but sometimes ovoid. Balls are used in ball games, where play follows the ball as it is hit, kicked or thrown, and in simpler activities such as catching and juggling. Balls made of hard-wearing materials form ball bearings, which provide very low [[Friction|friction]] bearings in engineering. Black-powder weapons used stone and metal balls as projectiles. Rubber balls were unknown outside the [[Americas]] until after the voyages of Columbus. The most ancient balls in [[Eurasia]] were found in Karasahr, China, and are about 3,000 years old; they were made of hair-filled leather.

Rare, unexplained luminous spherical phenomenon, usually associated with [[Thunderstorm|thunderstorms]]. Reported objects range from pea-sized to several meters across and last considerably longer than a lightning flash. It is distinct from [[St. Elmo's fire]]. Some 20th-century reports describe balls that explode and leave an odor of [[Sulfur|sulfur]]. Scientific data remain scarce, and laboratory experiments have produced similar visual effects, but how they relate to the phenomenon remains unclear.

Form of verse, often a narrative set to music. Ballads were characteristic of popular poetry and song in [[England]], Ireland and [[Scotland]] from the Late Middle Ages until the 19th century, and they spread across Europe and later to North America, South America and Australia. Ballads have no prescribed structure, but many use quatrains with ABCB or ABAB rhyme schemes. Originally written to accompany dances, they remained an oral tradition until collectors such as Bishop Thomas Percy published them. Most have no known author or correct version. Scottish ballads such as "Tam Lin" include supernatural elements. From the 18th century, poets including [[Samuel Taylor Coleridge]] wrote lyrical ballads.

Form of performance dance originating in the Italian Renaissance. It developed into a concert dance form in France and Russia, and its technical vocabulary underlies many other dance genres. Under the influence of [[Catherine de' Medici]], it spread to France. [[Louis XIV]] founded the Académie Royale de Danse in 1661 to set standards and certify instructors. In 1672 he made Jean-Baptiste Lully director of the Paris Opera, from which the first professional ballet company arose. Ballet declined in France after 1830 but continued in Denmark, Italy and Russia. The arrival in Europe of Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes on the eve of World War I revived interest and started the modern era. Notable 20th-century dancers include [[Anna Pavlova]], [[Rudolf Nureyev]] and [[Mikhail Baryshnikov]].

Ancient projectile weapon, sometimes called a bolt thrower. It developed from earlier Greek devices, using two levers with twisted-skein torsion springs in place of the bow of a [[Crossbow|crossbow]]. Early versions fired heavy darts or stones for [[Siege|siege warfare]]. The earliest form is thought to have been developed for Dionysius of Syracuse, around 400 BC. [[Philip II of Macedon|Philip II]] and [[Alexander the Great|Alexander]] made it both a siege engine and field artillery. The [[Roman Republic]] adopted and standardized the design, and larger models hurled stones of one talent (about 26 kg) up to 400 meters. The ballista remained in use into the Byzantine era and was supplanted by gunpowder artillery in the 15th century.

Field of [[Mechanics|mechanics]] concerned with the launching, flight behavior and impact effects of projectiles, especially weapon munitions. The word derives from the Greek *ballein*, "to throw." A ballistic missile is guided only during the brief initial powered phase, after which its trajectory is governed by classical mechanics. Ballistics was placed on a mathematical basis by [[Isaac Newton]] in *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica* (1687), whose laws of motion and gravity made trajectories predictable. Galileo had derived the parabolic form of the ballistic trajectory in 1638. Modern applications include weapon design, forensic linking of projectiles to firearms, and safety protocols.

Unpowered aerostat that remains aloft due to its buoyancy. A balloon may use hot air or a gas lighter than air, such as [[Hydrogen]] or [[Helium]]. Unlike an [[Airship]], it cannot propel itself, but its altitude can be adjusted to find favorable winds. The [[Montgolfier brothers]] built the first passenger-carrying balloon, a [[Hot air balloon|hot air balloon]], in Annonay, France, in 1783, and the first passenger flight carried a sheep, a duck and a rooster. Hydrogen was used extensively at first, but after the [[Hindenburg disaster]] it was seldom used because of its flammability. Helium is used for all airships and most manned gas balloons.

Set of partner dances enjoyed socially and competitively around the world. The term derives from the Latin *ballare*, "to dance." Ballroom was once social dancing for the privileged, and balls featured dances such as the minuet, quadrille, polonaise, polka and mazurka. Competitive ballroom, known as DanceSport, has two main schools. The International School has Standard dances, including the [[Waltz|waltz]] and [[Tango|tango]], and Latin dances including samba, cha cha, rumba, paso doble and jive. The American School, most common in the United States, has Smooth and Rhythm categories.

Province of [[Pakistan]], the largest by land area and the least populated. Balochistan is an extensive plateau of rough terrain, bordering [[Iran]] to the west and [[Afghanistan]] to the north, with a coastline on the [[Arabian Sea]] to the south. The province makes up about 44% of Pakistan's land area, but only 5% of it is arable, and agriculture and livestock make up about 47% of its economy. The name means "land of the Baloch people." Since 2004 a Baloch insurgency, led by groups including the Baloch Liberation Army, has used bombings and ambushes. Critics argue that resource extraction has benefited the federal government more than local development.

Arm of the [[Atlantic Ocean]] in northern Europe, enclosed by nine countries. It is the world's largest [[Brackish water|brackish water]] basin, with salinity averaging about 7 parts per thousand because of large freshwater inflows. It drains through the Danish Straits into the [[Kattegat]] and has limited water exchange with the Atlantic, making it an inland sea. Its gulfs include the Gulf of Bothnia, the Gulf of Finland and the Gulf of Riga. Canals connect it to the White Sea and, through the [[Kiel Canal]], to the North Sea. The [[Hanseatic League]] dominated trade in timber, grain and fish from the 13th to 17th centuries. Nutrient runoff from agriculture and wastewater fosters harmful algal blooms and oxygen depletion.

Geopolitical term for Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania on the eastern coast of the [[Baltic Sea]]. All three are members of [[NATO]] and the [[European Union]]. Independent in 1918, they were occupied and annexed by the [[Soviet Union]] in 1940, occupied by [[Nazi Germany]] in 1941, and re-occupied by the Soviets in 1944. They regained independence in 1991 as the Soviet Union disintegrated. All three are classified as high-income economies by the World Bank.

Most populous city in the U.S. state of [[Maryland]]. Baltimore had a population of 585,708 at the 2020 census, and its metropolitan area had 2.86 million residents. It was designated an independent city by the Constitution of Maryland in 1851. The Port of Baltimore was established in 1706 to support the [[Tobacco|tobacco]] trade with Europe. Baltimore briefly served as the nation's capital during the [[American Revolutionary War]]. The Battle of Baltimore was pivotal in the [[War of 1812]], and the British bombardment of Fort McHenry inspired Francis Scott Key to write the poem "The Star-Spangled Banner," designated the U.S. national anthem in 1931. The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, the nation's oldest, was built in 1830.

Siberian husky and sled dog (c. 1919–March 14, 1933). Balto was credited as leader of the team on the final leg of the 1925 serum run to Nome, Alaska, which carried [[Diphtheria|diphtheria]] antitoxin from [[Anchorage, Alaska]]. The team was driven by Gunnar Kaasen, and Balto became a celebrity, with a statue in [[Central Park]] and a [[Vaudeville]] tour. After the dogs were sold to a circus and kept in poor conditions in Los Angeles, a fundraising effort in [[Cleveland]] bought them in 1927. Balto lived at the Cleveland Zoo until his death, and his body is displayed at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History. His role has since been reappraised.

American [[Skateboarding|skateboarder]], stunt performer and television personality. He rose to prominence as a cast member of the [[MTV]] stunt series *Jackass* (2000–2001) and its films. He created the spin-off *Viva La Bam* (2003–2006) and co-wrote and directed the films *Haggard* (2003) and *Minghags* (2009). He was a playable character in the *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater* video game series. Margera has struggled with alcoholism and legal problems since the mid-2000s, and in 2021 he was fired from production of *Jackass Forever* (2022) because of drug and alcohol issues.

Capital and largest city of [[Mali]] (pop., 2022: 4,227,569), on the [[Niger River]]. Bamako is the nation's administrative center and lies near rapids that divide the upper and middle Niger valleys. It is the seventh-largest urban center in [[West Africa]], after [[Lagos]], Abidjan, [[Kano (city)|Kano]], Ibadan, Dakar and Accra. Its manufactures include textiles, processed meat and metal goods. The area was settled in the Paleolithic era, and in 1883 the French established a fort there. A railroad to Kayes was built in 1904, and Bamako became capital of French Sudan in 1908. Mali gained independence from France in April 1960.
